policies.policy_name: Delete Change Request Mapping – Role Authorization
policies.description: Only users with the Administrator, Manager, or Agent role may delete change‑request‑mapping records; all other users (e.g., Reporter) must be denied with a 403 Forbidden error.
references: Administrator (admin) | System Configuration & Integrity | Full CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) access across all tables.
Manager (manager) | Supervision, Escalation, Approvals | Full CRUD on operational tables (incident, problem, change, knowledge); READ access to all the tables.
Agent (agent) | Frontline Incident/Request fulfillment | Full CRUD on Incidents, Service Requests, Tasks, Work Notes, CMDB, Change, Problem, and Knowledge. READ access to all the tables.

Reporter (reporter) | IT Service Consumption | Can view and update their own submitted Incidents/Requests. Can search Public Knowledge articles. | Cannot view or modify records opened by other users, CMDB, or internal work notes.
403 Forbidden: Permission denied (user role lacks authority for the operation).

policies.description: Before invoking **delete_change_request_mappings**, verify that the request payload contains at least one mandatory filter key (`change_request_mapping_id`, `change_id`, `incident_id`, or `problem_id`). Call **list_change_request_mappings** with the same filter set; if the call returns an empty list, abort and raise a policy violation. If the call returns one or more mappings, proceed with the deletion. (If the system provides a field such as `locked` or a `status` indicating a non‑deletable state, optionally check that field and abort when it signals a locked mapping.) This version relies only on the existence of the list operation and does not assume any undocumented attributes.
references: • Atomic Operations: Perform one validated operation at a time, except when using approved batch endpoints. Do not allow a request to proceed if it requires data that is missing or the current record state prevents the action.
• Mandatory Fields: Any request to create or update a record must validate all mandatory fields.
• Policy Violation: If a user request violates any rule herein, you must halt the operation and provide the specific policy reason before pausing.

policies.description: When using the **delete_change_request_mappings** tool, first call one of the read‑only mapping tools (list_change_request_mappings, find_change_request_mappings_for_incident, or find_change_request_mappings_for_problem) with the same filter criteria you intend to use for deletion. Count how many mappings exist that involve the same change ID and the same incident ID or problem ID. If the count is 1 (i.e., the mapping you would delete is the only link between that change and the incident/problem), refuse the deletion and return a policy‑violation message. Otherwise, proceed with the delete_change_request_mappings call.
references: Referential Integrity: Before closing any record, verify that all mandatory dependencies are satisfied.

policies.description: Only users with the **Administrator** role may invoke the `delete_change_request_mappings` tool. If the caller’s role is anything other than Administrator (e.g., Manager, Agent, Reporter), the request must be stopped and a **403 Forbidden** response returned, without executing the tool.
references: | **Administrator** (admin) | System Configuration & Integrity | Full CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) access across all tables. |
403 Forbidden: Permission denied (user role lacks authority for the operation).

policies.description:
Before invoking **delete_change_request_mappings**, enforce the following checks using only available ITSM tools and data:
1. Verify the requester’s role is **admin** or **manager** via `get_user` or `list_users`.
2. Confirm that the request includes at least one of the required filter fields (`change_request_mapping_id`, `change_id`, `incident_id`, `problem_id`).
3. Use `list_change_request_mappings` to ensure a mapping that satisfies **all** supplied filters actually exists.
If any of these validations fail, abort the deletion and return a clear policy‑violation message. (Any organization‑specific approval steps that cannot be validated programmatically should be handled outside this automated flow.)
references: First you must check the user information and operate exclusively based on confirmed user roles, verified record relationships, and ITIL/database integrity rules.
Policy Violation: If a user request violates any rule herein, you must halt the operation and provide the specific policy reason before pausing.
Referential Integrity: Before closing any record, verify that all mandatory dependencies are satisfied.
Mandatory Fields: Any request to create or update a record must validate all mandatory fields.

policies.description: Before calling the **delete_change_request_mappings** tool, first confirm that every identifier supplied in the request actually exists in the system. Use the appropriate lookup tools (e.g., `find_change_request_mappings_for_incident`, `find_change_request_mappings_for_problem`, `find_change_by_number`, `find_incident_by_id`, `find_problem_by_number`) to fetch the records. Only if the lookup returns a valid record should the delete operation be performed. Do not create or guess IDs; rely exclusively on the results of these verification calls.
references: First you must check the user information and operate exclusively based on confirmed user roles, verified record relationships, and ITIL/database integrity rules. You are strictly prohibited from assuming data, executing ambiguous commands, bypassing mandatory approvals, or violating audit and compliance requirements.
Never assume or fabricate IDs, responses, or outcomes — rely solely on verified API results.

policies.description: A delete_change_request_mappings call must include at least one filter parameter (change_request_mapping_id, change_id, incident_id, or problem_id). If no filter is supplied, halt the operation and report the missing mandatory filter.

For the `delete_change_request_mappings` tool, the request payload must contain at least one filter (`change_request_mapping_id`, `change_id`, `incident_id`, or `problem_id`). If multiple filters are supplied, the backend must apply **AND** logic—i.e., only mappings that match **all** supplied filters are eligible for deletion. The caller should construct the request accordingly and may pre‑validate the filter set before issuing the API call.

policies.policy_name: Work Log Requirement for Deletion Operations
policies.description: When invoking the **delete_change_request_mappings** tool, the assistant must ensure that an audit entry is recorded. If a **log_action** tool (or equivalent) is available, call it immediately after the deletion with parameters `action="delete_change_request_mappings"`, `resource_id` (the identifier(s) of the deleted mapping), `user_id` (the caller), and `timestamp` (current ISO‑8601 time). If no explicit logging tool exists, verify that the platform automatically creates an audit log for the deletion; if it does not, abort the operation and return the error “Work‑log requirement not satisfied”.
references: You are strictly prohibited from assuming data, executing ambiguous commands, bypassing mandatory approvals, or violating audit and compliance requirements.
All work logs must include the timestamp (created_on) and the user_id performing the action.

policies.policy_name: Rate Limiting Compliance for Deletion Operations
policies.description: If a delete_change_request_mappings request exceeds the allowed rate limit, pause the operation and retry using exponential backoff as defined by the system’s rate‑limiting policy.
references: Rate Limiting: If exceeded, pause and retry using Exponential Backoff.

archive.description: If a delete_change_request_mappings request encounters a 409 Conflict response (e.g., record locking or state conflict), abort the operation and report the conflict to the user.
references: 409 Conflict: Record locking or state conflict.

The policy directly mentions the target tool (delete_change_request_mappings) and therefore is both relevant and tool‑specific. Its enforcement can be performed after the tool call by checking the HTTP status code; no pre‑call validation is possible because lock state cannot be determined without invoking the tool. The instruction is clear and can be acted upon using only the tool's response and chat context, making it actionable. The policy is self‑contained – it provides enough detail to be understood without external information. Overall the policy is well‑written, though it could note that no retry should be attempted, which is a minor improvement. Score: 4/5.
